art-of-the-offer:q1.quote: Recommend and offer vaccines at the same visit. Research shows that when patients receive a vaccine recommendation and are offered the vaccine at the same time, they are more likely to be vaccinated.
art-of-the-offer:q1.claim: CDC says to recommend and offer vaccines at the same visit because patients who get both a recommendation and an offer are more likely to be vaccinated.
art-of-the-offer:q1.reason: Choice 2 recommends and offers both vaccines now. Choice 1 only asks a tentative question with no recommendation. The source omits the four-to-five-times figure.

art-of-the-offer:q10.quote: Health-care personnel should administer a dose of Tdap during each pregnancy irrespective of the patient’s prior history of receiving Tdap. To maximize the maternal antibody response and passive antibody transfer to the infant, optimal timing for Tdap administration is between 27 and 36 weeks of gestation although Tdap may be given at any time during pregnancy.
art-of-the-offer:q10.claim: CDC recommends Tdap in every pregnancy and times it to maximize passive transfer of maternal antibodies to the infant.
art-of-the-offer:q10.reason: The source says maternal vaccine antibodies pass to the infant. That is the deciding fact behind the better reply.

art-of-the-offer:q11.quote: Participate in your state's immunization registry. Help your office, your patients, and your patients' other providers know which vaccines your patients have had.
art-of-the-offer:q11.claim: Immunizers should use the state registry so the patient's other providers know which vaccines the patient has received.
art-of-the-offer:q11.reason: The CDC standard says to share vaccination records with the patient's other providers, which is the reassurance offered in the bank answer.

art-of-the-offer:q12.quote: Flu vaccines cannot cause flu. Side effects of the flu vaccine are generally mild and go away on their own within a few days.
art-of-the-offer:q12.claim: CDC states flu vaccines cannot cause flu and their side effects are usually mild and resolve on their own within a few days.
art-of-the-offer:q12.reason: The quote states both facts in the chosen reply: the vaccine cannot cause flu, and mild side effects go away within days.

art-of-the-offer:q13.quote: CDC recommends giving a single dose of Tdap during every pregnancy, preferably during the early part of gestational weeks 27 through 36.
art-of-the-offer:q13.claim: CDC recommends one dose of Tdap during every pregnancy, preferably early in weeks 27 through 36.
art-of-the-offer:q13.reason: A dose in every pregnancy means the earlier dose does not cover this pregnancy. That backs the repeat-booster choice.

art-of-the-offer:q14.quote: Pregnant women should get a single dose of the maternal RSV vaccine (Pfizer’s Abrysvo) during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy sometime between September through January.
art-of-the-offer:q14.claim: CDC says pregnant women should get one dose of Abrysvo during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy, between September and January.
art-of-the-offer:q14.reason: The recommended window is weeks 32 through 36, so at 24 weeks the right move is to schedule the dose rather than give it today.

art-of-the-offer:q15.quote: There is no specific amount of time you need to wait before administering Shingrix to patients who have had herpes zoster. However, you should not give Shingrix to patients who are experiencing an acute episode of herpes zoster.
art-of-the-offer:q15.claim: Patients who have had herpes zoster can receive Shingrix without a waiting period, just not during an acute episode.
art-of-the-offer:q15.reason: CDC says to vaccinate people with prior zoster once the acute episode is over. That backs the healed patient getting Shingrix and rules out the lifelong immunity reply.

art-of-the-offer:q16.quote: However, intervals between doses that are longer than recommended typically do not reduce final antibody concentrations, although protection might not be attained until the recommended number of doses has been administered. With some exceptions (e.g. oral typhoid vaccine) an interruption in the vaccination schedule does not require restarting the entire series of a vaccine or toxoid or addition of extra doses7.
art-of-the-offer:q16.claim: Longer than recommended intervals usually do not lower final antibody levels, and an interrupted schedule generally does not require restarting the series.
art-of-the-offer:q16.reason: CDC says a lapsed schedule needs no restart, and RZV is not a named exception, so giving the second dose now is correct.

art-of-the-offer:q18.quote: Heplisav-B For adults aged 18 years through adulthood People aged 18 years and older should receive two doses.
art-of-the-offer:q18.claim: The CDC says people aged 18 and older who get Heplisav-B should receive two doses.
art-of-the-offer:q18.reason: A two-dose adult Heplisav-B series means not every adult vaccine needs three shots, so choice 2 wins. The source never states the one-month interval.

art-of-the-offer:q19.quote: CDC recommends 2 doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV) to prevent shingles and related complications in adults aged ≥50 years.
art-of-the-offer:q19.claim: CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine for adults aged 50 and older to prevent shingles and its complications.
art-of-the-offer:q19.reason: A two-dose recommendation rules out skipping dose two, so the source settles the choice. It does not mention long-term duration or nerve pain specifically.

art-of-the-offer:q2.quote: If multiple vaccines are administered at a single visit, administer each preparation at a different anatomic site28. The location of all injection sites with the corresponding vaccine injected should be documented in each patient’s medical record.
art-of-the-offer:q2.claim: When several vaccines are given at one visit, CDC says each goes at a different anatomic site and each site is recorded with its vaccine.
art-of-the-offer:q2.reason: Separate sites with documented locations back one shot per arm. Injecting both right together in one spot fails the different-site rule.

art-of-the-offer:q20.quote: A 3-dose series is recommended for persons who receive the first valid dose on or after their 15th birthday, and for persons with primary or secondary immunocompromising conditions that might reduce cell-mediated or humoral immunity, such as B lymphocyte antibody deficiencies, T lymphocyte complete or partial defects, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, malignant neoplasm, transplantation, autoimmune disease, or immunosuppressive therapy, in whom immune response to vaccination may be attenuated.
art-of-the-offer:q20.claim: People who get their first valid HPV dose on or after their 15th birthday are recommended a 3-dose series.
art-of-the-offer:q20.reason: A 22-year-old starting the series is past 15, so the source requires three doses. Being under 26 does not qualify them for two.

art-of-the-offer:q4.quote: Recombinant and adjuvanted vaccines (like Shingrix) can be administered concomitantly at different anatomic sites with other adult vaccines. This includes COVID-19 vaccines.
art-of-the-offer:q4.claim: CDC says Shingrix can be given at the same visit as other adult vaccines, at different anatomic sites.
art-of-the-offer:q4.reason: Tdap is another adult vaccine, so giving it with Shingrix the same day is allowed. That rules out the four-week wait.

art-of-the-offer:q5.quote: RSV vaccines can be coadministered with other adult vaccines during the same visit.
art-of-the-offer:q5.claim: CDC says RSV vaccines can be given with other adult vaccines at the same visit.
art-of-the-offer:q5.reason: Same-visit coadministration with other adult vaccines rules out the "never together" choice and establishes the bank answer, though pneumococcal is not named specifically.

art-of-the-offer:q6.quote: With some exceptions, simultaneously administering the most widely used live and non-live vaccines has produced seroconversion rates and rates for adverse reactions similar to those observed when the vaccines are administered separately12151617.
art-of-the-offer:q6.claim: CDC says that, with some exceptions, giving common vaccines together produces immune responses and adverse reaction rates similar to giving them separately.
art-of-the-offer:q6.reason: Similar adverse reaction rates when vaccines are given together make the reassuring reply the better choice over calling simultaneous shots dangerous.

art-of-the-offer:q7.quote: Beginning with the 2023-2024 season, additional safety measures are no longer recommended for flu vaccination of people who are allergic to eggs beyond those recommended for receipt of any vaccine, regardless of the severity of previous reaction to egg. All vaccines should be administered in settings in which personnel and equipment needed for rapid recognition and treatment of allergic reactions are available.
art-of-the-offer:q7.claim: Since the 2023-2024 season, people with egg allergy of any severity need no extra safety measures for flu vaccination beyond those used for any vaccine.
art-of-the-offer:q7.reason: CDC says egg allergy of any severity needs no special precautions or hospital setting, so a routine flu shot is appropriate and Choice 1 is wrong.

art-of-the-offer:q8.quote: A person's risk for herpes zoster and related complications, including hospitalizations, sharply increases after 50 years of age. The reasons why VZV reactivates and causes herpes zoster are not well understood. However, a person's risk for herpes zoster increases as their VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity declines.
art-of-the-offer:q8.claim: Shingles risk rises sharply after age 50 and increases as VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity declines.
art-of-the-offer:q8.reason: CDC ties shingles risk to age over 50 and declining immunity, not fitness, which is the deciding fact for the better reply.

co-administration:q1.quote: In patients recommended to receive both PCV13 and PPSV23, the 2 vaccines should not be administered simultaneously28. PCV13 should be administered first. If PPSV23 has been administered first, PCV13 should be administered no earlier than 8 weeks later in children 6–18 years, and one year later in adults 19 years and older.
co-administration:q1.claim: The source says PCV13 and PPSV23 should not be given at the same visit when both are indicated, including for adults.
co-administration:q1.reason: The source lists adult exceptions to simultaneous administration, so the claim that all indicated adult vaccines can be given at one visit is wrong.

co-administration:q2.quote: With some exceptions, simultaneously administering the most widely used live and non-live vaccines has produced seroconversion rates and rates for adverse reactions similar to those observed when the vaccines are administered separately12151617.
co-administration:q2.claim: CDC says that giving the most widely used vaccines together, with some exceptions, produces seroconversion and adverse reaction rates similar to giving them separately.
co-administration:q2.reason: Seroconversion is similar when vaccines are given together, so the immune system is not overloaded or broadly suppressed. That makes the statement false.

co-administration:q3.quote: For infants and younger children, if more than 2 vaccines are injected in a single limb, the thigh is the preferred site because of the greater muscle mass; the injections should be sufficiently separated (separate anatomic sites [i.e. ≥1 inch] if possible) so that any local reactions can be differentiated1329.
co-administration:q3.claim: CDC says multiple injections in a single limb should be separated by at least 1 inch so local reactions can be told apart.
co-administration:q3.reason: CDC states same-limb injections should be at least 1 inch apart, which matches the TRUE answer. The passage is framed for infants and younger children.

co-administration:q4.quote: Concomitant administration of RZV with Fluarix Quadrivalent (influenza vaccine) (QIV) has been studied, and there was no evidence for interference in the immune response to either vaccine or safety concerns (32).
co-administration:q4.claim: Studies of giving RZV together with quadrivalent influenza vaccine found no evidence that either vaccine interfered with the immune response to the other.
co-administration:q4.reason: The source reports no interference with the immune response to either vaccine, so the claim of impaired responses is false.

co-administration:q5.quote: Simultaneously administering all vaccines for which a person is eligible at the time of a visit increases the probability that a child, adolescent, or adult will be vaccinated fully by the appropriate age13.
co-administration:q5.claim: Giving all eligible vaccines at one visit makes it more likely a person is fully vaccinated by the appropriate age.
co-administration:q5.reason: The source covers simultaneous administration and coverage but never mentions presumptive recommendations or how recommendation style affects patient acceptance.

co-administration:q7.quote: If multiple vaccines are administered at a single visit, administer each preparation at a different anatomic site28. The location of all injection sites with the corresponding vaccine injected should be documented in each patient’s medical record.
co-administration:q7.claim: CDC says the location of every injection site, along with the vaccine given there, should be documented in the patient's medical record.
co-administration:q7.reason: The quote directly says each injection site and its vaccine should be recorded in the medical record, which makes the statement true.

co-administration:q8.quote: Although there is no exact limit on the number of injections, with a little flexibility, a provider can ensure that the primary series doses are given without administering too many injections at each visit.
co-administration:q8.claim: CDC says there is no exact limit on injections and providers can use schedule flexibility to avoid giving too many at one visit.
co-administration:q8.reason: The source suggests flexibility about injection numbers but never covers handling a patient's hesitation, addressing concerns, or documenting a refusal.

flagship-r2:q17.quote: Shingles on the face can affect the eye and cause vision loss.
flagship-r2:q17.claim: The CDC says shingles on the face can affect the eye and cause vision loss.
flagship-r2:q17.reason: The source confirms eye involvement can cause vision loss. It does not say the loss is permanent or that it is an ophthalmologic emergency.

flagship:q1.quote: About 1 in 2 people with hepatitis B do not know they are infected.
flagship:q1.claim: CDC states that about one in two people with hepatitis B do not know they are infected.
flagship:q1.reason: One in two is about half, which matches the statement exactly, so the TRUE answer holds.

flagship:q10.quote: CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for children younger than 5 years and adults 50 years or older.
flagship:q10.claim: CDC recommends pneumococcal vaccination for all adults aged 50 years or older.
flagship:q10.reason: The recommendation is based on age alone, so a healthy adult becomes routinely eligible at 50. That matches the TRUE answer.

flagship:q13.quote: The following conditions increase the risk of severe RSV illness:A Chronic cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart failure, coronary artery disease, or congenital heart disease [excluding isolated hypertension])
flagship:q13.claim: CDC lists chronic cardiovascular disease, including heart failure, as a condition that increases the risk of severe RSV illness.
flagship:q13.reason: Heart failure appears as its own risk condition, listed separately from chronic lung disease, so it raises risk without lung disease.

flagship:q14.quote: People with egg allergy may receive any flu vaccine (egg-based or non-egg-based) that is otherwise appropriate for their age and health status.
flagship:q14.claim: CDC says people with egg allergy may receive any flu vaccine, egg-based or not, that fits their age and health status.
flagship:q14.reason: Egg-based vaccines are explicitly allowed for egg-allergic people, so the statement is false, matching the bank answer.

flagship:q19.quote: Administering Tdap during each pregnancy helps protect infants during the time when they're most vulnerable. Optimal timing is between 27 and 36 weeks gestation, preferably during the earlier part of this period. Vaccination during each pregnancy is important for transferring the greatest number of protective antibodies to each infant.
flagship:q19.claim: CDC says to give Tdap during each pregnancy so that each infant gets the most protective antibodies.
flagship:q19.reason: The source says to vaccinate during each pregnancy with no spacing exception. It does not mention closely spaced pregnancies by name.

flagship:q20.quote: Flu vaccination has been associated with lower rates of some cardiac events among people with heart disease, especially among those who have had a cardiac event in the past year.
flagship:q20.claim: Flu vaccination is associated with fewer cardiac events in people with heart disease, especially after a recent cardiac event.
flagship:q20.reason: The quote supports only the cardiac part. The HPV source covers infections and cancers, but no single passage establishes all three parts.

flagship:q8.quote: Vaccines given with a needle at the same visit should be given at separate places on the body (at least one inch apart). Adults and older children can get them in the same arm at least an inch apart, or they can get them in different arms.
flagship:q8.claim: CDC says injected vaccines given at one visit can go in the same arm if the sites are at least an inch apart.
flagship:q8.reason: The source allows the same arm when sites are at least one inch apart. That shows the statement is false, matching the bank answer.

flagship:q9.quote: Is infectious for at least 7 days on surfaces.
flagship:q9.claim: The CDC states that hepatitis B virus is infectious for at least 7 days on surfaces.
flagship:q9.reason: The CDC lists HBV as infectious for at least 7 days on surfaces, which matches the TRUE answer exactly.

hepatitis-b:q1.quote: These include AS01B (in Shingrix, recombinant zoster subunit vaccine) (119), MF59 (in Fluad Quadrivalent [aIIV4]) (120), and cytosine phosphoguanine oligodeoxynucleotide (in Heplisav-B, a recombinant hepatitis B surface antigen vaccine) (121).
hepatitis-b:q1.claim: The source lists Heplisav-B, a recombinant hepatitis B vaccine, among the licensed vaccines that contain nonaluminum adjuvants.
hepatitis-b:q1.reason: This source covers influenza vaccines. It names a hepatitis B vaccine only in passing and never covers universal adult hepatitis B vaccination for ages 19 through 59.

hepatitis-b:q2.quote: The Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommends hepatitis B (HepB) vaccination among all infants at birth, unvaccinated children younger than 19 years of age, adults aged 19–59 years, and adults aged 60 years and older with risk factors for hepatitis B or without identified risk factors but seeking protection.
hepatitis-b:q2.claim: ACIP recommends HepB vaccination for adults 60 and older who have risk factors and also for those without identified risk factors who seek protection.
hepatitis-b:q2.reason: Adults 60 and older without risk factors may get vaccinated if they seek protection, so a risk factor is not required.

hepatitis-b:q3.quote: HEPLISAV-B is indicated for prevention of infection caused by all known subtypes of hepatitis B virus. HEPLISAV-B is approved for use in adults 18 years of age and older.
hepatitis-b:q3.claim: HEPLISAV-B prevents infection by all known hepatitis B subtypes and is approved for adults 18 years of age and older.
hepatitis-b:q3.reason: The source confirms the adult age range and the adjuvanted name, but never states the two-dose, one-month-apart schedule.

hepatitis-b:q4.quote: In multivariate analyses that considered persons without hepatitis B–related risk behaviors (i.e., injection-drug use, male sex with a male, and sex with multiple partners), persons aged 23 through 59 years with diabetes had 2.1 (95% confidence interval [CI] = 1.6–2.8) times the odds of developing acute hepatitis B as those without diabetes; the odds were 1.5 (CI = 0.9–2.5) times as likely for persons aged ≥60 years.
hepatitis-b:q4.claim: Adults aged 23 through 59 with diabetes had 2.1 times the odds of acute hepatitis B compared with adults without diabetes.
hepatitis-b:q4.reason: The source shows adults with diabetes face higher, not lower, hepatitis B risk, so the statement is false as the bank answer says.

hepatitis-b:q5.quote: New recommendations include hepatitis B screening using three laboratory tests at least once during a lifetime for adults aged ≥18 years.
hepatitis-b:q5.claim: CDC's 2023 recommendations call for hepatitis B screening with three laboratory tests at least once in a lifetime for all adults aged 18 and older.
hepatitis-b:q5.reason: The quote states that CDC recommends lifetime screening of all adults aged 18 and older with three tests, which matches the statement.

hepatitis-b:q6.quote: However, intervals between doses that are longer than recommended typically do not reduce final antibody concentrations, although protection might not be attained until the recommended number of doses has been administered. With some exceptions (e.g. oral typhoid vaccine) an interruption in the vaccination schedule does not require restarting the entire series of a vaccine or toxoid or addition of extra doses7.
hepatitis-b:q6.claim: Longer than recommended intervals do not require restarting a vaccine series, with exceptions such as oral typhoid vaccine.
hepatitis-b:q6.reason: CDC says an interrupted schedule does not require restarting the series. Hepatitis B is not listed as an exception, so the statement is false.

hepatitis-b:q7.quote: Although there is no hepatitis D vaccine, getting hepatitis B vaccine also protects you from hepatitis D.
hepatitis-b:q7.claim: The CDC says there is no hepatitis D vaccine, but the hepatitis B vaccine also protects against hepatitis D.
hepatitis-b:q7.reason: The CDC says outright that hepatitis B vaccine protects against hepatitis D, so the TRUE answer holds.

hepatitis-b:q8.quote: Generally, clinicians will treat people with acute hepatitis B with supportive care depending on the symptoms. There are several antiviral medications available for chronic hepatitis B. It is important to link these patients to care with regular monitoring to prevent liver damage and/or hepatocellular carcinoma.
hepatitis-b:q8.claim: Chronic hepatitis B is managed with antiviral medications and linkage to care with regular monitoring.
hepatitis-b:q8.reason: The source never addresses vaccinating or boosting HBsAg-positive people, so it neither confirms nor refutes annual boosters.

hpv:q1.quote: During clinical trials before the licensure, the 9-valent HPV vaccine Gardasil 9 was studied in more than 15,000 males and females and was found to be safe and effective.
hpv:q1.claim: Gardasil 9 is a 9-valent HPV vaccine that was studied in more than 15,000 males and females before licensure and found safe and effective.
hpv:q1.reason: The source calls Gardasil 9 nine-valent but never names its HPV types or splits them into high-risk and wart-causing groups.

hpv:q2.quote: ACIP also recommends vaccination for everyone through age 26 years if not adequately vaccinated when younger. HPV vaccination is given as a series of either two or three doses, depending on age at initial vaccination.
hpv:q2.claim: ACIP recommends HPV vaccination for everyone through age 26 who was not adequately vaccinated when younger.
hpv:q2.reason: A recommendation for everyone shows vaccination is not limited to females, so the statement is false. The source does not address male cancers.

hpv:q3.quote: A 2-dose series is recommended for persons who receive the first valid dose before their 15th birthday (except for persons with certain immunocompromising conditions). The second and final dose should be administered 6 through 12 months after the first dose (0, 6-12 month schedule).
hpv:q3.claim: People who get their first HPV dose before age 15 need 2 doses, with the second given 6 to 12 months after the first.
hpv:q3.reason: The source states a 2-dose series for anyone starting before age 15, with the second dose 6 to 12 months later. Only immunocompromised people are excepted.

hpv:q4.quote: Adults aged >26 years. Catch-up HPV vaccination is not recommended for all adults aged >26 years. Instead, shared clinical decision-making regarding HPV vaccination is recommended for some adults aged 27 through 45 years who are not adequately vaccinated.
hpv:q4.claim: ACIP recommends shared clinical decision-making about HPV vaccination for some adults aged 27 through 45 years who are not adequately vaccinated.
hpv:q4.reason: The recommendation directly names shared clinical decision-making for inadequately vaccinated adults aged 27 through 45, which makes the statement true.

hpv:q5.quote: Vaccination will provide less benefit to sexually active persons who have been already infected with one or more HPV vaccine types. However, HPV vaccination can provide protection against HPV vaccine types not already acquired.
hpv:q5.claim: People already infected with some HPV vaccine types get less benefit, but vaccination still protects against vaccine types they have not acquired.
hpv:q5.reason: Past HPV infection reduces but does not eliminate benefit, so the statement that all benefit is lost is false, matching the bank answer.

hpv:q6.quote: Bednarczyk RA, Davis R, Ault K, et al. Sexual activity-related outcomes after human papillomavirus vaccination of 11- to 12-year-olds. Pediatrics. 2012;130(5):798-805.
hpv:q6.claim: The page cites a 2012 Pediatrics study on sexual activity outcomes after HPV vaccination of 11 to 12 year olds.
hpv:q6.reason: The page only lists study titles on sexual behavior. It never states whether vaccination changes sexual debut or contraceptive use.

hpv:q7.quote: HPV vaccination does not eliminate the need for continued cervical cancer screening, since up to 30% of cervical cancers are caused by HPV types not prevented by the quadrivalent or bivalent vaccines, and 15% of cervical cancers are caused by HPV types not prevented by the 9-valent vaccine.
hpv:q7.claim: HPV vaccination does not remove the need for continued cervical cancer screening because some cervical cancers come from HPV types the vaccines do not cover.
hpv:q7.reason: The source says outright that vaccination does not eliminate screening, so the statement is false.

hpv:q8.quote: If a woman is found to be pregnant after starting the HPV vaccine series, second and/or third doses should be delayed until they are no longer pregnant. If a woman receives HPV vaccine and later learns that she is pregnant, there is no reason to be alarmed.
hpv:q8.claim: CDC says a pregnancy found mid-series only means delaying the remaining doses until after pregnancy, and there is no reason for alarm.
hpv:q8.reason: CDC's only action is to delay the remaining doses and it says there is no reason for alarm, so termination is not indicated. The statement is false.

influenza:q1.quote: Routine annual influenza vaccination as described in the July 2025 immunization schedule. All persons should receive an FDA-licensed age-appropriate influenza vaccine (one that is approved for their age), with the exception that solid organ transplant recipients aged 18 through 64 years who are receiving immunosuppressive medication regimens may receive either HD-IIV3 or aIIV3 as acceptable options (without a preference over other age-appropriate IIV3s or RIV3) (see Immunocompromised Persons, below).
influenza:q1.claim: The page points to the July 2025 schedule for routine annual flu vaccination and says everyone who gets a flu vaccine should get one licensed for their age.
influenza:q1.reason: The page defers to the July 2025 schedule. It never names the 6 months and older universal group or attributes that recommendation to ACIP.

influenza:q2.quote: The overall cumulative hospitalization rate was 17.3 per 100,000 population, with the highest rate among adults aged ≥65 years (50.0), followed by children aged 0–4 years (21.9), adults aged 50–64 years (16.0), children and adolescents aged 5–17 years (9.0), and was lowest among adults aged 18–49 years (9.1).
influenza:q2.claim: During 2021–22, adults aged 65 and older had the highest cumulative influenza hospitalization rate of any age group.
influenza:q2.reason: This surveillance report never mentions preferential vaccines for adults 65 and older, Fluzone High-Dose, Flublok or adjuvanted vaccines.

influenza:q3.quote: Egg allergy does not indicate additional safety measures for flu vaccination beyond those recommended for any recipient of any vaccine, regardless of severity of previous reaction to egg.
influenza:q3.claim: CDC says egg allergy of any severity calls for no safety measures beyond those used for every vaccine recipient.
influenza:q3.reason: A longer observation period would be an additional safety measure, and CDC says none is needed regardless of egg reaction severity.

influenza:q4.quote: IIV has been available since the 1940s. Most influenza vaccines distributed in the United States are subvirion (split-virus) or subunit inactivated vaccines.
influenza:q4.claim: Most US influenza vaccines are split-virus or subunit inactivated vaccines.
influenza:q4.reason: The source describes inactivated and recombinant vaccine composition but never states that flu shots cannot cause influenza.

influenza:q5.quote: For most persons who need only 1 dose of influenza vaccine for the season, vaccination should ideally be offered during September or October.
influenza:q5.claim: CDC says most people who need only one flu vaccine dose should ideally be vaccinated in September or October.
influenza:q5.reason: The quote directly states September or October as the ideal timing for most people, matching the TRUE answer.

influenza:q6.quote: Adults and children who have chronic pulmonary (including asthma), cardiovascular (excluding isolated hypertension), renal, hepatic, neurologic, hematologic, or metabolic disorders (including diabetes mellitus).
influenza:q6.claim: People with chronic cardiovascular disorders are listed as a group at higher risk for medical complications from influenza.
influenza:q6.reason: The source lists heart disease as a risk group but never says vaccination reduces cardiac events in people with heart disease.

influenza:q7.quote: Moderate or severe acute illness (with or without fever) in a patient is considered a precaution to vaccination, although persons with minor illness may be vaccinated.
influenza:q7.claim: Only moderate or severe acute illness is a precaution to influenza vaccination, and people with minor illness may be vaccinated.
influenza:q7.reason: A mild afebrile cold counts as a minor illness, which the source says may be vaccinated, so postponing is not required.

influenza:q8.quote: Administration of any IIV3 or RIV3 to persons receiving influenza antiviral medications for treatment or chemoprophylaxis of influenza is acceptable.
influenza:q8.claim: Inactivated or recombinant flu vaccine can be given to people who are taking flu antivirals for treatment or prevention.
influenza:q8.reason: The source never says antivirals are not a substitute for vaccination. It only allows giving vaccine alongside antivirals and mentions chemoprophylaxis for people who cannot be vaccinated.

pneumococcal:q1.quote: Administer PCV15, PCV20, or PCV21 for all adults 50 years or older Who have never received any pneumococcal conjugate vaccine Whose previous vaccination history is unknown
pneumococcal:q1.claim: The CDC routinely recommends a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine for all adults 50 or older who have never had one or whose history is unknown.
pneumococcal:q1.reason: The source sets routine conjugate vaccination at age 50 for adults with no prior conjugate dose. It credits CDC, not ACIP by name.

pneumococcal:q3.quote: Active immunization for the prevention of pneumonia caused by S. pneumoniae serotypes 1, 3, 4, 5, 6A, 6B, 7F, 8, 9V, 10A, 11A, 12F, 14, 15B, 18C, 19A, 19F, 22F, 23F, and 33F in individuals 18 years of age and older.
pneumococcal:q3.claim: Prevnar 20 is approved to prevent pneumococcal pneumonia from 20 serotypes in people 18 years and older.
pneumococcal:q3.reason: The source covers only the Prevnar 20 indications. It does not mention Capvaxive, the single-dose schedule, or whether PPSV23 follow-up is needed.

pneumococcal:q4.quote: Many conditions are an indication for pneumococcal vaccination for both children and adults: Cerebrospinal fluid leak Chronic liver disease Cochlear implant An immunocompromising condition Diabetes mellitus
pneumococcal:q4.claim: CDC lists diabetes mellitus as a risk condition that indicates pneumococcal vaccination for adults.
pneumococcal:q4.reason: Diabetes is a listed adult risk indication, and the 19 through 49 guidance applies to risk conditions. So waiting until 50 is wrong.

pneumococcal:q5.quote: The overall case-fatality rate for bacteremia is about 20%. It may be as high as 60% among patients who are older adults.
pneumococcal:q5.claim: Pneumococcal bacteremia kills about 20% of patients overall and up to 60% of older adult patients.
pneumococcal:q5.reason: CDC lists bacteremia as a serious pneumococcal syndrome with up to 60% fatality in older adults, which shows substantial mortality in that group.

pneumococcal:q6.claim: The cited source is the CDC 2022 opioid prescribing guideline and contains nothing about pneumococcal vaccines.
